keyVerseText: And when all the captains of the armies, they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah governor, there came to Gedaliah to Mizpah, even Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan the son of Careah, and Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah the son of a Maachathite, they and their men.
rootMeaning: The root of קָרֵחַ (Qârêach) comes from the Hebrew verb קָרַח (qârach), which means 'to be bald' or 'to make bald.' This root conveys the literal sense of baldness or hairlessness, a physical characteristic that is rare and distinctive. Understanding this root meaning enriches the name Qârêach by highlighting a concrete, visual trait—baldness—that likely identified the individual or family line, beyond a mere label.
usageInScripture: The word קָרֵחַ appears 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily as a proper name, with 13 occurrences translated as 'of Kareah' and one as 'of Careah.' This consistency shows that the term is used almost exclusively as a personal or family name rather than a descriptive adjective. The name identifies a particular Israelite figure, the father of Johanan and Jonathan, who played a significant role in supporting Gedaliah’s leadership after the Babylonian exile, indicating the name's historical and narrative importance.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, the name Qârêach rooted in 'baldness' reminds us that God often uses ordinary, even physically distinctive individuals, to accomplish His sovereign purposes. The baldness implied by the name may symbolize vulnerability or humility, yet this man’s family was instrumental in preserving God's people during a crisis. This teaches believers that God’s strength is made perfect in human weakness, and that He calls and raises up leaders from all walks of life to fulfill His redemptive plan. It also underscores the providential care God extends to His covenant community, even in exile and hardship.
keyVerseReflection: In 2 Kings 25:23, Johanan the son of Careah is mentioned among the leaders who come to support Gedaliah, the Babylonian-appointed governor. The inclusion of 'son of Careah' identifies Johanan’s lineage and connects him to a family known for loyalty and action during a turbulent time. This detail highlights the continuity of God's people through faithful families and leaders, even in captivity, and shows how God’s providence works through personal and familial identity to sustain His purposes.
